name: Ben Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Ben. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the office side of a small letting agency, five of us in a shopfront on the main road. I book viewings, draw up tenancy agreements from templates, log deposits, chase references and handle the repair emails from tenants. I use AI tools all day: one drafts the property adverts, another sorts my inbox. I'm still new to the legal side, and my manager Debbie checks every tenancy agreement I do.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like fixing a slow process. I got viewings booked by text instead of phone and it cut no-shows in half. What wears me out is landlords who want everything yesterday. I live with my partner Zara, who's a teaching assistant, and we've got under a month's money saved, which bugs me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are handy and people should just use them sensibly. I'd post something showing how I use them, because I think that's more useful than arguing about hype. At work I'd keep doing what I'm doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'm a bit ahead of everyone else, and that stays true for a while. That's good for me at a small agency. But the money's still the money: junior pay, few agencies in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write a short guide for the office on how we use the tools, so Debbie sees it as my thing. I'd ask about the lettings qualification, because that gets you a better grade. And I'd set up an automatic transfer of fifty pounds a month into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm about the tech. The bank balance is another story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use the tools all day. What's the gap between the hype and what they actually do for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The adverts are great, the legal stuff's useless. The AI wrote a lovely advert for a flat with a garden, and the flat didn't have a garden. So I check everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Under a month saved bugs you. What's the plan for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fifty a month, automatic, so I don't think about it. And I'd stop buying lunch at the bakery, which Zara keeps telling me to do.

say: I'd say the tools are **handy** and should be used **sensibly**.
I'd post how I use them rather than **argue about hype**.
think: Privately I'm **a bit ahead** of everyone else, which helps at a small agency.
The **junior pay** and few local agencies are the real limits.
do: Write a short **AI guide** for the office.
Ask about the **lettings qualification** for a better grade.
Set up an automatic **fifty pounds** a month into savings.
feel: **Calm** about the tech, less so about the **bank balance**.
S0.quote: The AI wrote a lovely advert for a flat with a garden, and the flat didn't have a garden.
fieldNote: Ben feels **ahead of the curve** and uses that to stand out at work.
His humour about the **garden advert** shows he checks AI output carefully.
Money, not technology, is his **real pressure**.

steps.text: Write a short guide to the agency's AI tools
Start the lettings qualification for a better grade
Set up an automatic fifty pounds a month into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good news for anyone willing to learn, and I'd mean it. Online I'd share the tools that actually work. At the agency I'd offer to run the switch-over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job splits in two. The booking and the paperwork go to software. What's left is the person who handles awkward landlords and gets the tools working, and I'd want to be that person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the lettings qualification in the first six months. I'd ask Debbie to put me on property inspections too, because that's visits and judgment, not just forms. I'd also start doing AI setups for two other small agencies on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but excited too. Honestly more excited than nervous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Debbie checks your work now. What if the software checks it instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then Debbie's job changes as well. If software checks every tenancy agreement, our letting agency needs fewer people in the office, and I'd make sure I'm the one who runs it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you look if the agency shrank?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's only one other agency in town, and they're smaller. So probably the side work, or moving to the city with Zara, which she doesn't want.

say: I'd say it's **good news** for anyone willing to learn.
At the agency I'd offer to **run the switch-over**.
think: Privately my job **splits in two**: paperwork goes, people work stays.
I'd want to be the one who **runs the tools**.
do: Finish the **lettings qualification** in six months.
Ask Debbie for **property inspection** work, which needs visits.
Set up AI tools for **two other agencies** on the side.
S1.quote: If software checks every tenancy agreement, our letting agency needs fewer people in the office, and I'd make sure I'm the one who runs it.
fieldNote: Ben sounds upbeat, but he expects **fewer office jobs** at the agency.
He heads toward **inspections**, which are hands-on, sensing they last longer.
A **city move** is his fallback, though Zara is against it.

steps.text: Finish the lettings qualification within six months
Ask Debbie for property inspection visits
Set up AI tools for two other agencies for a fee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's huge and we need a plan as a country, quickly. I'd probably post about what people can do in the next year. At the agency I'd try to keep everyone calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the agency goes down to Debbie and a system. Being good with the tools won't matter when the tools don't need anyone. I'd be one of many.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push to do as many inspections as possible, since someone still has to walk round a flat. I'd sell my side work hard for the first year, while small firms are confused. And I'd cut back properly: no car, no holidays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's the speed that gets me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The card says robots come about three years after the thinking AI. Does that help inspections?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a bit. Walking round a flat checking for damp might be my job until 2031, and then a robot does that too. So it buys three years, not a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Zara say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Zara would say her school still needs teaching assistants, and we'd live on hers. That's probably right for a while. I'd hate it, though.

say: I'd say we need a **national plan**, quickly, and I'd post about next steps.
At the agency I'd try to keep everyone **calm**.
think: Privately the agency drops to **Debbie and a system**.
Being good with tools **won't matter** when they need no one.
do: Take on as many **inspections** as possible.
Sell my **side work** hard in the first year.
S2.quote: Walking round a flat checking for damp might be my job until 2031, and then a robot does that too.
fieldNote: Even Ben's early-adopter edge **disappears** in two years.
He sees **inspections** as three extra years, not a career.
He'd lean on **Zara's wage**, which he finds hard to accept.

steps.text: Take on as many property inspections as possible
Sell AI setup work to confused small firms
Sell the car and skip holidays for a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a real warning, so use it. I'd be the one at the agency saying let's plan. Online I'd share what I was doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'd have time to build something of my own. Maybe a tiny lettings business that runs on AI, with me doing the visits. It's risky, but I'm fine with risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd finish the qualification and save hard, maybe a hundred a month. In year two I'd take on a couple of landlords myself on the side. By year four I'd decide whether to go full time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a good way, if that makes sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years. What would you be in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A landlord or two who'd trust me. I'd rather run a tiny lettings business with AI doing the paperwork than be the last admin at someone else's agency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you'd want to take now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, going on my own. Zara would worry, but she'd see the point once I showed her the numbers.

say: I'd say five years is a **real warning**, so use it.
At the agency I'd be the one saying **let's plan**.
think: Privately I'd have time to build **something of my own**.
A tiny **AI-run lettings business** with me doing visits is risky but possible.
do: Finish the **qualification** and save about **a hundred** a month.
Take on **two landlords** on the side in year two.
Decide on going **full time** by year four.
S3.quote: I'd rather run a tiny lettings business with AI doing the paperwork than be the last admin at someone else's agency.
fieldNote: Five years lets Ben think like an **owner** rather than staff.
His plan **uses AI** for paperwork and keeps visits for himself.

steps.text: Save about a hundred pounds a month
Take on two landlords of my own in year two
Use AI to handle the tenancy paperwork for my landlords

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and people who start now will be fine. I'd probably be a bit preachy about it, honestly. At work I'd be the AI guy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do well out of this one. Ten years is enough to build a small business and pay off some debt. The end point still worries me, but I'd be ready-ish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the qualification, save for two years, then start the business slowly with a few landlords. I'd use AI for every bit of paperwork. I'd keep my job until the business pays the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly. More hope than fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Is that enough for your own agency?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. I'd have time to get it right and make mistakes early. Zara could stay at the school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell younger people coming into admin now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say learn the tools, but also learn the people bit, because that's what lasts. Anyone can get an AI to write a tenancy agreement, but a tenant crying about a broken boiler wants a person.

At work I'd be the **AI guy**, a bit preachy.
think: Privately I'd **do well** out of this one.
The **end point** still worries me, but I'd be ready-ish.
do: Save for **two years**, then start a small **lettings business**.
Keep the job until the business **pays the rent**.
S4.quote: Anyone can get an AI to write a tenancy agreement, but a tenant crying about a broken boiler wants a person.
fieldNote: Ben sees **opportunity** in the decade, unlike most of his peers.
He advises learning **the people bit**, which he values most.
He still names the **end point** as a worry.

steps.text: Save for two years before starting a business
Start a small lettings business with a few landlords
Run all tenancy paperwork through AI tools

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd be ahead for six months and then just another person who's good with tools nobody needs to be good with. What would help is some breathing room: a few months of pay while people work out what's next.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people who are excited about AI. Being the AI person in the office feels like a safe seat until you notice the seat is also on the list.

headlineQuote: Being the AI person in the office feels like a safe seat until you notice the seat is also on the list.
portrait: Ben is a **27-year-old** junior administrator at a small letting agency.
He uses **AI tools daily** and enjoys fixing slow processes.
He lives with Zara, a **teaching assistant**, on very little savings.
He's comfortable with **risk** and leans toward running his own small lettings business.
His mood is mostly uneasy or anxious, turning **alarmed** only under AGI by 2028.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when his early start lasts only months.
whatWouldHelp: A few months of **pay** while people work out what's next.
